pumac-2020-finals-b-01.title: Pigeonhole on row sums
pumac-2020-finals-b-01.body:
**Answer: exactly the pairs with $n\le k$.** (A path visits each cell at most once.)

**If $n>k$ the property fails.** Fill the rightmost column with $1$'s and every other cell with $0$'s. Every path from the left edge to the right edge contains at least one and at most $k$ cells of the rightmost column, so its sum is between $1$ and $k<n$, never a multiple of $n$.

**If $n\le k$ the property holds.** Let $R_i$ be the sum of the numbers in row $i$ and $S_j=R_1+\dots+R_j$ for $j=1,\dots,k$.
- If some $S_j\equiv0\pmod n$, then rows $1,\dots,j$ have total sum divisible by $n$.
- Otherwise the $k$ numbers $S_1,\dots,S_k$ have residues among $1,\dots,n-1$; since $k\ge n>n-1$, two of them agree, $S_i\equiv S_j$ with $i<j$, and then $R_{i+1}+\dots+R_j\equiv0\pmod n$.
In both cases there are consecutive rows $a,\dots,b$ whose total sum is a multiple of $n$. Now walk column by column: in column $1$ move vertically through all cells of rows $a,\dots,b$ (starting at row $a$), step right to column $2$ at the row where you ended, move through rows $a,\dots,b$ in the opposite direction, step right again, and so on. This path starts in the leftmost column, ends in the rightmost column, and visits every cell of rows $a,\dots,b$ exactly once, so its sum is $R_a+\dots+R_b\equiv0\pmod n$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2020-finals-b-02.title: $M=4040$
pumac-2020-finals-b-02.body:
We show $M=4040$ works.

**Case $p<4040^2$.** Take $n=p$. Then $p\bmod n=0\le\frac n{2020}$, $n=p\ge\sqrt p$, and $n=\sqrt p\cdot\sqrt p<4040\sqrt p=M\sqrt p$.

**Case $p\ge4040^2$.** The interval $\left[\frac{\sqrt p}{4040},\frac{\sqrt p}{2020}\right]$ has length $\frac{\sqrt p}{4040}\ge1$, so it contains an integer $q\ge1$. Let $n=\left\lfloor\frac{p-1}q\right\rfloor$ and $r=p-qn$; by the definition of the floor, $1\le r\le q$.
- *Upper bound:* $n<\frac pq\le\frac{p}{\sqrt p/4040}=4040\sqrt p$.
- *Lower bound:* $n\ge\frac{p-q}{q}=\frac pq-1\ge2020\sqrt p-1\ge\sqrt p$ (as $q\le\frac{\sqrt p}{2020}$).
- *Residue:* $p=qn+r$ with $0\le r<n$ (indeed $r\le q\le\frac{\sqrt p}{2020}<\sqrt p\le n$), so dividing $p$ by $n$ leaves remainder $r$. Therefore
$$p\bmod n=r\le q\le\frac{\sqrt p}{2020}\le\frac n{2020}.$$
So in both cases the required $n$ exists. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2020-finals-b-03.title: Radical-type lemma, then the antipode
pumac-2020-finals-b-03.body:
Let $\Gamma$ be the circumcircle of $ABC$ (centre $O$, radius $R$). We use directed angles mod $180^\circ$ and assume $D\ne B$, $E\ne C$ (so the circles in the statement are defined).

**Lemma.** For $X\in\Gamma$ distinct from $B,C$, let $Y$ be the second intersection of circles $BDX$ and $CEX$ ($Y=X$ if they are tangent). Then $Y$ lies on line $DE$.
*Proof.* Using $BDXY$ and $CEXY$ cyclic, and $D\in AB$, $E\in AC$:
$$\angle(DY,YE)=\angle(DY,YX)+\angle(XY,YE)=\angle(DB,BX)+\angle(XC,CE)=\angle(AB,BX)+\angle(XC,CA).$$
Since $A,B,C,X\in\Gamma$, $\angle(AB,BX)=\angle(AC,CX)$, so the sum equals $\angle(AC,CX)+\angle(XC,CA)=0$. Hence $D,Y,E$ are collinear. $\square$

**Statement 1 $\iff$ line $DE$ meets $\Gamma$.**
($\Rightarrow$) If the circles are tangent at $X$, then $Y=X$ and by the lemma $X\in DE$, so $X\in DE\cap\Gamma$.
($\Leftarrow$) Let $X\in DE\cap\Gamma$ (with $X\ne B,C$; $X\ne D,E$ since $D,E\notin\Gamma$ unless degenerate). The line $DE$ meets circle $BDX$ only at $D$ and $X$, and circle $CEX$ only at $E$ and $X$. By the lemma $Y\in DE$ lies on both circles, so $Y\in\{D,X\}\cap\{E,X\}=\{X\}$ (as $D\ne E$). So $Y=X$: the circles meet only at $X$, i.e. they are tangent there.

**Line $DE$ meets $\Gamma$ $\iff AB\cdot AD\le4R^2$.** Since $BCED$ is cyclic, $DE$ is antiparallel to $BC$ in the angle at $A$; the tangent to $\Gamma$ at $A$ is also antiparallel to $BC$, so $DE$ is parallel to the tangent at $A$, i.e. $DE\perp AA'$ where $A'$ is the antipode of $A$. Let $H=DE\cap AA'$, the projection of $D$ onto line $AA'$. A line perpendicular to the diameter $AA'$ meets $\Gamma$ iff its foot $H$ lies on the segment $AA'$. Since $D$ is on ray $AB$, $H$ is on ray $AA'$ at distance
$$AH=AD\cos\angle BAA'=AD\cdot\frac{AB}{AA'}=\frac{AD\cdot AB}{2R},$$
because $\angle ABA'=90^\circ$ (it subtends the diameter). Thus $H\in AA'$ iff $AH\le2R$ iff $AB\cdot AD\le4R^2$.

Combining the two equivalences proves the claim. $\blacksquare$
